messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 50-year-old South Asian animator, came to therapy after a year in which sleep, work, and family life had narrowed around the memory of his son’s medical crisis. The ordeal began when his child developed a sudden, life-threatening illness and was rushed into the hospital, where Ravi spent long nights sitting beside a monitor, watching nurses move quickly through procedures he did not understand and breathing in the sharp antiseptic smell that now seemed to him inseparable from danger. What frightened him most was not only how close his son came to dying, but how helpless he felt while strangers performed examinations and interventions that determined whether his child lived. Since then, the most ordinary reminders of that period had taken on a force he could not shake: an unfamiliar bed when traveling for animation work, the silence of sleeping alone when his wife was away, the sterile odor of a clinic corridor, or the sight of a medical exam room door left half-open could pull him back into the same dread.

In the months after his son recovered, Ravi found that these moments did not simply unsettle him; they pushed him into a pattern of mental strain he described as trying to stay one step ahead of catastrophe. If he had to sleep alone or in a hotel room for a work trip, he would lie awake rehearsing every possible emergency, turning over worst-case scenarios in his mind until he felt vaguely prepared, as if imagining the disaster in advance might make it less shocking. When a family member mentioned a checkup or when he had to accompany his child to a follow-up visit, the medical procedures themselves became difficult to bear, and afterward he would spend hours thinking about how powerless he had been and even ruminating about revenge against the illness, as though there were someone to punish for what had nearly happened. At the same time, he repeatedly asked his wife, his siblings, and even colleagues to reassure him that he was okay, that his son was okay, that nothing hidden was about to go wrong. These habits gave him momentary relief, but they also kept the hospital nights alive in his mind, because each round of reassurance or mental rehearsal pulled him back to the same fearful scenes and made the old triggers feel even closer.

Over time, Ravi began organizing his days around avoiding anything that might set that process off again. He declined assignments that would require overnight travel, because sleeping alone in an unfamiliar place felt too similar to those nights in the hospital when he had sat awake waiting for news. He became increasingly tense around clinics and would hurry his family through hallways that smelled of antiseptic, sometimes turning his face away as if that could keep the memories from landing. Even at home, the cycle continued: a single conversation about a doctor’s appointment could send him back into worst-case rehearsal, which left him needing more reassurance and more certainty than his family could give. The more he tried to prepare himself by mentally replaying threats or asking others to calm him, the more he seemed to notice potential dangers everywhere, and the more any reminder of the hospital threatened to seize his attention.

His wife had started to notice how much of his emotional energy was being consumed by these loops. Ravi, once easygoing and absorbed in his drawings, now checked and rechecked plans, avoided being alone at night when he could, and carried a low-level fear that something disastrous could return without warning. He remained especially vulnerable to the combination of unfamiliar sleeping arrangements and medical reminders, because both carried him back to the helplessness he felt when his son was critically ill. After another business trip in which he barely slept in a hotel room and spent the night mentally running through emergencies, he finally sought help, saying he was exhausted by living as if he had to brace for the next hospital call at all times. What he most feared was being caught unprepared if his son became ill again; what he most hoped for was to sleep without scanning for danger, and to sit in a doctor’s office or a strange room without feeling that the old crisis was about to begin again.
